proofs.proof_tex:
Let
\[
\mathscr D=\{\gamma\in[1,\infty):\mathcal F_{\gamma}(H)\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
We first use monotonicity of the displayed sensitivity inequalities.  If
\(1\le\gamma\le\gamma'<\infty\) and \(x\in\mathcal F_{\gamma}(H)\), then, coordinate by coordinate,
\[
(\gamma')^{-1}r_a(m\mid c)q_a(c,s)
\le \gamma^{-1}r_a(m\mid c)q_a(c,s)
\le \lambda_a(c,s,m)
\le \gamma r_a(m\mid c)q_a(c,s)
\le \gamma' r_a(m\mid c)q_a(c,s).
\]
Here nonnegativity of \(r_a\) and \(q_a\) justifies both comparisons.  All equality constraints are independent of \(\gamma\), so \(x\in\mathcal F_{\gamma'}(H)\).  Thus \(\mathscr D\) is upward closed.

We next use compactness of finite probability tables.  Summing the projection equations over \(c,m,z_m\), and using the definition of the identified response laws together with known randomization, assignment positivity, and \(0<\nu<\infty\), gives
\[
\sum_{c,m,z_m}H_a(c,m,z_m)
=\nu^{-1}\mathbb E\!\left[e_a(B_i)^{-1}\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}N_i\right]
=\nu^{-1}\mathbb E[N_i]=1.
\]
Consequently every feasible table satisfies
\[
\sum_{c,s,m}\lambda_a(c,s,m)=1,
\qquad
\sum_{c,s}q_a(c,s)=1,
\qquad
\sum_{c,s_0,s_1}\pi(c,s_0,s_1)=1.
\]
All coordinates of \(x\) therefore lie in \([0,1]\).  Because the state spaces are finite and all constraints are closed, every \(\mathcal F_{\gamma}(H)\) is compact.

Suppose \(\mathscr D\ne\varnothing\), and put \(\gamma_0=\inf\mathscr D\).  Since every element of \(\mathscr D\) is finite, \(1\le\gamma_0<\infty\).  Choose \(\gamma_n\in\mathscr D\) with \(\gamma_n\to\gamma_0\), and choose \(x_n\in\mathcal F_{\gamma_n}(H)\).  The preceding common bound gives a convergent subsequence, say \(x_n\to x_0\).  The equality rows pass to the limit.  Since \(\gamma_0\ge1\), both coefficient maps \(\gamma\mapsto\gamma\) and \(\gamma\mapsto\gamma^{-1}\) are continuous at \(\gamma_0\); hence every two-sided sensitivity inequality also passes to the limit.  Thus \(x_0\in\mathcal F_{\gamma_0}(H)\), so the onset is attained.  Upward closure then gives \(\mathscr D=[\gamma_0,\infty)\).  If \(\mathscr D=\varnothing\), its infimum is \(\infty\) by definition; conversely, any member of \(\mathscr D\) would make its infimum finite.  This proves all assertions, including that an index below the onset is an infeasible restriction rather than a causal conclusion.

Fix a finite \(\Gamma\ge\Gamma_{\mathrm{feas}}\).  By Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:feasibility\mbox{-}onset}\), the feasible polytope is nonempty.  Let \(\Theta_I^{\Gamma}(H)\) denote the set of all values of \(\beta\) generated by cluster potential-outcome and vector-response laws that preserve the observed distribution of \(B_i\), reproduce \(H_0,H_1\), obey the known randomized assignment and the stated causal assumptions, and satisfy the \(\Gamma\)-selection restriction.  We prove sharpness by an outer-map argument followed by an explicit reverse embedding.

First consider any compatible cluster potential-outcome and response law.  On each positive-mass stratum define its individual-weighted finite tables by
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_a(c,s,m)
&=\mathbb P^{\star}\{C_i=c,Y_{ij}(a)=s,M_{ij}(a)=m\},\\
q_a(c,s)
&=\mathbb P^{\star}\{C_i=c,Y_{ij}(a)=s\},\\
\pi(c,s_0,s_1)
&=\mathbb P^{\star}\{C_i=c,Y_{ij}(0)=s_0,Y_{ij}(1)=s_1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
These tables are nonnegative, and marginalization gives \(q_a(c,s)=\sum_m\lambda_a(c,s,m)\) and the two displayed coupling-marginal equations in \(\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H)\).

We next verify the observed-law rows.  Cluster SUTVA and observation consistency identify the realized record under \(A_i=a\) with \((M_{ij}(a),\operatorname{pr}_{M_{ij}(a)}Y_{ij}(a))\).  Conditional randomization and the known assignment probability give, for every \(c,m,z_m\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_a(c,m,z_m)
&=\nu^{-1}\mathbb E\!\left[
e_a(B_i)^{-1}\mathbf 1\{A_i=a,C_i=c\}
\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}\mathbf 1\{M_{ij}(a)=m,
\operatorname{pr}_mY_{ij}(a)=z_m\}\right]\\
&=\mathbb P^{\star}\{C_i=c,M_{ij}(a)=m,
\operatorname{pr}_mY_{ij}(a)=z_m\}\\
&=\sum_{s:\operatorname{pr}_m(s)=z_m}\lambda_a(c,s,m).
\end{aligned}
\]
The inverse assignment weight is well defined because assignment positivity gives \(e_a(B_i)\ge\varepsilon>0\), and the expectation is finite because \(N_i\) has finite mean.  For a cell with \(q_a(c,s)>0\), the pattern-selection assumption and the identity
\[
\lambda_a(c,s,m)
=q_a(c,s)\mathbb P^{\star}\{M_{ij}(a)=m\mid C_i=c,Y_{ij}(a)=s\}
\]
give exactly
\[
\Gamma^{-1}r_a(m\mid c)q_a(c,s)
\le\lambda_a(c,s,m)
\le\Gamma r_a(m\mid c)q_a(c,s).
\]
When \(q_a(c,s)=0\), nonnegativity and marginalization force every corresponding \(\lambda_a(c,s,m)\) to be zero, so the same inequalities hold.  Hence the law maps to a point \(x\in\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H)\).  Moreover,
\[
\beta
=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_+}\sum_{(s_0,s_1)\in R}\pi(c,s_0,s_1)
=c_R^{\mathsf T}x.
\]
If \(c\notin\mathcal C_+\), then \(\mathbb P^{\star}(C_i=c)=\kappa(c)=0\), so this omitted stratum contributes neither to the displayed probability nor to any constraint.  This proves the outer inclusion
\[
\Theta_I^{\Gamma}(H)\subseteq[L_{\Gamma},U_{\Gamma}].
\]

For the reverse inclusion, fix an arbitrary \(x=(\lambda_0,\lambda_1,q_0,q_1,\pi)\in\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H)\).  Summing its projection equations gives, for every \(c\in\mathcal C_+\),
\[
\sum_s q_a(c,s)
=\sum_{m,z_m}H_a(c,m,z_m)
=\kappa(c),
\]
where the last equality follows from the inverse-randomization calculation above with the additional indicator \(\mathbf 1\{C_i=c\}\).  The coupling rows therefore imply \(\sum_{s_0,s_1}\pi(c,s_0,s_1)=\kappa(c)\).  Define
\[
p_c(s_0,s_1)=\frac{\pi(c,s_0,s_1)}{\kappa(c)}
\]
and, whenever \(q_a(c,s)>0\),
\[
\rho_a(m\mid c,s)=\frac{\lambda_a(c,s,m)}{q_a(c,s)}.
\]
Marginalization makes \(p_c\) and each such \(\rho_a\) probability mass functions.  When \(q_a(c,s)=0\), choose any probability mass function for \(\rho_a(\cdot\mid c,s)\); that choice is on a null event.

We now construct a cluster superpopulation.  Draw \(B_i\), including its complete labeled roster and \(N_i\), from its observed preassignment distribution.  Notice that \(\kappa(c)=\nu^{-1}\mathbb E[N_i\mathbf 1\{C_i=c\}]=0\), together with \(N_i\ge1\), implies \(\mathbb P(C_i=c)=0\).  Thus a realized baseline record lies in a stratum in \(\mathcal C_+\) almost surely.  For a realized record with \(C_i=c\in\mathcal C_+\), and for every roster label \(j\), draw
\[
(Y_{ij}(0),Y_{ij}(1))\sim p_c,
\]
and then draw \(M_{ij}(a)\) from \(\rho_a(\cdot\mid c,Y_{ij}(a))\), for \(a=0,1\).  Conditional independence across labels and arms is one valid choice; no maintained restriction requires it.  Draw \(A_i\) conditionally on \(B_i\) with the known probability \(e_a(B_i)\), independently of all potential variables, and define the realized record by observation consistency.  Repeat this construction independently across clusters.  Thus the constructed records are identically distributed and independent, preserve the entire observed distribution of \(B_i\), obey cluster SUTVA, obey the known randomized assignment, and satisfy positivity.

To verify its individual-weighted law, for any function \(f\) of one roster member, the definition of size weighting gives
\[
\mathbb E^{\star}[f]
=\nu^{-1}\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{j=1}^{N_i}f_{ij}\right].
\]
Since every conditional draw in a stratum uses \(p_c\),
\[
\mathbb P^{\star}\{C_i=c,Y_{ij}(0)=s_0,Y_{ij}(1)=s_1\}
=\nu^{-1}\mathbb E[N_i\mathbf 1\{C_i=c\}]p_c(s_0,s_1)
=\pi(c,s_0,s_1).
\]
Multiplication by \(\rho_a\) similarly yields
\[
\mathbb P^{\star}\{C_i=c,Y_{ij}(a)=s,M_{ij}(a)=m\}
=q_a(c,s)\rho_a(m\mid c,s)
=\lambda_a(c,s,m).
\]
The projection equations therefore reproduce \(H_a\).  Dividing the two sensitivity inequalities by \(q_a(c,s)>0\) shows that the constructed conditional response probability \(\rho_a(m\mid c,s)\) satisfies the maintained \(\Gamma\)-selection restriction; division is never used on a zero-mass cell.  Finally its causal probability is \(c_R^{\mathsf T}x\).  This establishes that every feasible objective value is generated by a compatible cluster law.

The feasible set is a nonempty compact convex polytope: compactness was established in the proof of Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:feasibility\mbox{-}onset}\), and convexity follows because all displayed constraints are linear at fixed \(\Gamma\).  Hence the minimum and maximum defining \(L_{\Gamma}\) and \(U_{\Gamma}\) are attained.  If \(x_L\) and \(x_U\) attain them, then for every \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
x_t=(1-t)x_L+t x_U\in\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H),
\qquad
c_R^{\mathsf T}x_t=(1-t)L_{\Gamma}+tU_{\Gamma}.
\]
The reverse embedding applied to \(x_t\) attains every point of the interval.  Thus
\[
\Theta_I^{\Gamma}(H)=[L_{\Gamma},U_{\Gamma}]=\mathcal I_{\Gamma}(H),
\]
which is sharp, not merely an outer bound.

It remains to derive the displayed certificates.  We use finite-dimensional polyhedral duality with the signs checked directly.  For the minimization problem, any unrestricted \(\alpha\) and \(\eta\ge0\) satisfying
\(E^{\mathsf T}\alpha-G_{\Gamma}^{\mathsf T}\eta\le c_R\) obey, for every feasible \(x\),
\[
\bar h^{\mathsf T}\alpha
=x^{\mathsf T}E^{\mathsf T}\alpha
\le x^{\mathsf T}c_R+x^{\mathsf T}G_{\Gamma}^{\mathsf T}\eta
\le c_R^{\mathsf T}x.
\]
Thus the proposed dual is a lower certificate.  To establish equality and attainment, append a slack vector \(z\ge0\), write \(G_{\Gamma}x+z=0\), introduce a scalar \(v\), and apply finite elimination to
\[
Ex=\bar h,
\qquad
G_{\Gamma}x+z=0,
\qquad
x,z\ge0,
\qquad
c_R^{\mathsf T}x\le v.
\]
Here finite elimination is elementary: for one variable, existence is equivalent to every lower bound being no larger than every upper bound, together with the inequalities not containing that variable; cross-multiplication uses only nonnegative coefficients.  Repeating this operation eliminates all coordinates of \(x,z\) without changing the projection.  Because the original feasible set is nonempty and compact, its projection on the \(v\)-coordinate is exactly the closed ray \([L_{\Gamma},\infty)\).  Consequently the finite eliminated system contains a lower inequality binding at \(v=L_{\Gamma}\).  Tracing the nonnegative combinations used to produce that inequality assigns unrestricted multipliers to the two equality orientations, nonnegative multipliers \(\eta\) to the sensitivity rows, and coefficient one to the objective row.  Cancellation of every eliminated nonnegative coordinate is precisely
\[
E^{\mathsf T}\alpha-G_{\Gamma}^{\mathsf T}\eta\le c_R,
\]
while the surviving constant is \(\bar h^{\mathsf T}\alpha=L_{\Gamma}\).  Thus a dual optimizer exists and equality holds.

Apply the same argument to minimization of \(-c_R^{\mathsf T}x\), and then replace the unrestricted equality multiplier by its negative.  The result is
\[
U_{\Gamma}
=\min_{\alpha\ \mathrm{unrestricted},\ \eta\ge0}
\left\{\bar h^{\mathsf T}\alpha:
E^{\mathsf T}\alpha+G_{\Gamma}^{\mathsf T}\eta\ge c_R\right\},
\]
with an attained optimizer.  Together with the preceding lower formula, these are the asserted finite-dimensional certificates.

Assume \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{feas}}<\infty\).  The coordinatewise comparison in the proof of Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:feasibility\mbox{-}onset}\) gives
\[
\mathcal F_{\gamma}(H)\subseteq\mathcal F_{\gamma'}(H)
\quad\text{whenever}\quad
\Gamma_{\mathrm{feas}}\le\gamma\le\gamma'<\infty.
\]
Minimizing the same linear objective over nested sets therefore gives \(L_{\gamma'}\le L_{\gamma}\).

Let
\[
\mathscr B=\{\gamma\in[1,\infty):
\exists x\in\mathcal F_{\gamma}(H),\ c_R^{\mathsf T}x\le1/2\}.
\]
This set is upward closed by the same nesting argument, and its infimum is \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{maj}}\) by definition.  If \(\mathscr B\ne\varnothing\), repeat the compactness-and-continuity argument used for the feasibility onset, now retaining the additional closed inequality \(c_R^{\mathsf T}x\le1/2\).  It follows that \(\mathscr B=[\Gamma_{\mathrm{maj}},\infty)\), so a finite majority threshold is attained.

For every feasible finite \(\gamma\), compactness and the sharpness theorem give
\[
\gamma\in\mathscr B
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
L_{\gamma}\le\frac12
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{some compatible law has }\beta\le\frac12.
\]
If \(\gamma<\Gamma_{\mathrm{maj}}\) is feasible, membership in \(\mathscr B\) fails.  Since the minimum is attained, this is equivalent to \(L_{\gamma}>1/2\), and sharpness then forces \(\beta>1/2\) under every compatible law.  At and above a finite threshold, membership in \(\mathscr B\) and the reverse embedding from the sharpness theorem supply a compatible law with \(\beta\le1/2\).  If \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{maj}}=\infty\), \(\mathscr B\) is empty, so the strict inequality holds at every finite feasible index.  Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:feasibility\mbox{-}onset}\) separately shows that indices below \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{feas}}\) are incompatibilities, not majority conclusions.

Finally suppose that every entry of \(H_a\), and hence every \(r_a(m\mid c)\), is rational, and let \(\delta>0\) be rational.  At any positive rational trial value \(\gamma\), both predicates
\[
\mathcal F_{\gamma}(H)\ne\varnothing
\quad\text{and}\quad
\exists x\in\mathcal F_{\gamma}(H):c_R^{\mathsf T}x\le1/2
\]
are finite rational linear-feasibility problems and are therefore exactly decidable by finite elimination or a rational-pivot linear-program algorithm.  Starting at one and doubling the trial value finds an upper bracket whenever the corresponding threshold is finite; monotonicity then permits bisection until the rational bracket has width at most \(\delta\).  If a threshold is infinite, the successive failed trials remain valid increasing lower bounds, although this search need not terminate with a certificate of infinity.  This proves the stated, explicitly qualified computability claim.

Let \(m_{\mathrm{all}}=(1,\ldots,1)\).  Under complete response, the definition of \(H_a\) gives
\[
H_a(c,m,z_m)=0\quad(m\ne m_{\mathrm{all}}),
\qquad
H_a(c,m_{\mathrm{all}},s)
=\mathbb P^{\star}\{C_i=c,Y_{ij}(a)=s\}.
\]
Consequently \(r_a(m_{\mathrm{all}}\mid c)=1\) and \(r_a(m\mid c)=0\) for every other pattern.  For \(m_{\mathrm{all}}\), the projection \(\operatorname{pr}_{m_{\mathrm{all}}}\) is the identity.  Its projection row therefore forces
\[
\lambda_a(c,s,m_{\mathrm{all}})=H_a(c,m_{\mathrm{all}},s).
\]
Every other projection right-hand side is zero, so nonnegativity forces \(\lambda_a(c,s,m)=0\) when \(m\ne m_{\mathrm{all}}\).  The completion equation now yields the point identification
\[
q_a(c,s)=\sum_m\lambda_a(c,s,m)
=H_a(c,m_{\mathrm{all}},s),
\]
which is the meaning of \(q_a=H_a\) in the complete-response reduction.

At \(\Gamma=1\), the sensitivity inequalities for the full pattern reduce to \(q_a\le\lambda_a\le q_a\), and those for every zero-frequency pattern reduce to \(0\le\lambda_a\le0\); all hold by the preceding identities.  For any finite \(\Gamma\ge1\), the full-pattern inequalities are
\[
\Gamma^{-1}q_a(c,s)\le q_a(c,s)\le\Gamma q_a(c,s),
\]
and all other pattern inequalities again say that zero equals zero.  Hence they impose no additional restriction.

For each \(c\in\mathcal C_+\), both fixed arm marginals have mass
\[
\sum_s q_a(c,s)=\sum_{m,z_m}H_a(c,m,z_m)=\kappa(c).
\]
Therefore a stratum-preserving coupling exists; for example,
\[
\pi(c,s_0,s_1)=
\frac{q_0(c,s_0)q_1(c,s_1)}{\kappa(c)}
\]
is well defined because \(\kappa(c)>0\).  Thus \(\mathcal F_1(H)\ne\varnothing\), and since the sensitivity index is restricted to \([1,\infty)\), the feasibility onset equals one.  After eliminating the forced \(\lambda_a\) and \(q_a\), the only remaining variables are precisely the nonnegative couplings \(\pi\) with these fixed arm marginals.  Minimizing and maximizing the strict-Pareto cost \(\mathbf 1_R\) over that transport polytope is the ordinary sharp finite optimal-transport interval.  The joint sharpness theorem proves that this optimization interval, rather than merely an outer relaxation, equals \(\mathcal I_{\Gamma}(H)\) for every finite \(\Gamma\ge1\).

theorem.statement:
For the complete-response pattern family, the signed system represented by \(\mathfrak H_R\) projects to two polynomial-size bipartite flow networks.  Write \(m_{\mathrm{all}}=(1,\ldots,1)\), put \(\mu_{a,c}(s)=H_a(c,m_{\mathrm{all}},s)=q_a(c,s)\), and, for any relation \(Q\subseteq\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\), define \(Q(A)=\{s_1:\exists s_0\in A,(s_0,s_1)\in Q\}\) and
\[
D_Q=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_+}\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal S}
\{\mu_{0,c}(A)-\mu_{1,c}(Q(A))\}.
\]
Then, for every finite \(\Gamma\ge1\),
\[
L_{\Gamma}=D_{R^{\mathsf c}},
\qquad
U_{\Gamma}=1-D_R.
\]
One minimum cut in the network containing exactly the \(R\)-edges returns an upper-attaining coupling and a maximizing family of sets in \(D_R\); a second minimum cut containing exactly the \(R^{\mathsf c}\)-edges returns a lower-attaining coupling and a maximizing family of sets in \(D_{R^{\mathsf c}}\).  Each network has \(O(|\mathcal C_+||\mathcal S|)\) vertices and \(O(|\mathcal C_+||\mathcal S|^2)\) edges.  If the entries of \(H_a\) are rational, multiplication by a common denominator yields integral capacities, integral extremal couplings, and integral cut certificates.  This is a complete network characterization for the complete-response family; no network-representability claim is made here for overlapping partial-response patterns.
theorem.proof_tex:
By Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:complete\mbox{-}response\mbox{-}reduction}\), the arm marginals \(\mu_{a,c}\) are fixed, have common stratum mass \(\kappa(c)\), and the only remaining choice is their stratum-preserving coupling.  We derive the network formula for an arbitrary relation \(Q\), then apply it to \(R\) and its complement.

Build a directed network with a source \(o\), a sink \(t\), a control vertex \((c,s_0,0)\), and a treatment vertex \((c,s_1,1)\).  Give the arc \(o\to(c,s_0,0)\) capacity \(\mu_{0,c}(s_0)\), the arc \((c,s_1,1)\to t\) capacity \(\mu_{1,c}(s_1)\), and an arc \((c,s_0,0)\to(c,s_1,1)\) of capacity two whenever \((s_0,s_1)\in Q\).  Capacity two exceeds the total mass one, so no minimum cut uses such an arc.

For a family \((A_c:c\in\mathcal C_+)\), place \(o\), all control vertices indexed by \(A_c\), and all treatment vertices indexed by \(Q(A_c)\) on the source side.  The resulting cut has capacity
\[
\sum_c\{\mu_{0,c}(\mathcal S\setminus A_c)+\mu_{1,c}(Q(A_c))\}
=1-\sum_c\{\mu_{0,c}(A_c)-\mu_{1,c}(Q(A_c))\}.
\]
Conversely, in any cut of capacity at most one, if \(A_c\) is the set of control vertices on the source side, every vertex in \(Q(A_c)\) must also be on that side, or a capacity-two arc crosses.  Removing any additional treatment vertices cannot increase the cut.  Hence the minimum cut capacity is exactly \(1-D_Q\).

For completeness, the flow equality and the returned coupling follow from a direct augmenting-path argument.  A maximum flow exists because its feasible set is a compact finite polytope.  From a maximum flow, mark every vertex reachable from \(o\) along an arc having positive residual capacity.  The sink is not marked, since otherwise the flow could be increased along a simple augmenting path.  Flow conservation then shows that the value of the flow equals the capacity of the marked/unmarked cut: every forward arc across it is saturated and every reverse-crossing arc carries zero flow.  Since every flow value is bounded by every cut capacity, the maximum flow value is therefore
\[
v_Q=1-D_Q.
\]

Interpret the middle-arc flows as a partial coupling \(f_c(s_0,s_1)\) supported on \(Q\).  Its residual row and column masses are
\[
r_{0,c}(s_0)=\mu_{0,c}(s_0)-\sum_{s_1}f_c(s_0,s_1),
\qquad
r_{1,c}(s_1)=\mu_{1,c}(s_1)-\sum_{s_0}f_c(s_0,s_1).
\]
Their common total is \(1-v_Q=D_Q\), after summing across strata, and their totals agree separately within each stratum because the network has no cross-stratum arcs.  No \(Q\)-edge can join a positive residual row to a positive residual column: such an edge, together with the two positive residual outer capacities, would be an augmenting path.  Within each stratum having residual total \(d_c>0\), set
\[
g_c(s_0,s_1)=\frac{r_{0,c}(s_0)r_{1,c}(s_1)}{d_c};
\]
set \(g_c=0\) if \(d_c=0\).  Then \(g_c\) has the residual marginals and is supported on \(Q^{\mathsf c}\).  Thus \(\pi_Q=f+g\) is a full coupling with
\[
\pi_Q(Q)=v_Q=1-D_Q.
\]
The cut inequality already shows that no coupling can place more mass on \(Q\), so this value is sharp and the construction returns an extremal coupling.

Taking \(Q=R\) gives \(U_{\Gamma}=1-D_R\).  Taking \(Q=R^{\mathsf c}\) gives a coupling with the largest possible complement mass \(1-D_{R^{\mathsf c}}\), hence
\[
L_{\Gamma}=1-\max_{\pi}\pi(R^{\mathsf c})=D_{R^{\mathsf c}}.
\]
The two cut networks have the asserted numbers of vertices and arcs.  If all capacities are rational, scale them by a common denominator.  Starting from zero, augment by the minimum residual capacity on an augmenting path.  Integral capacities keep every flow integral and terminate after finitely many augmentations.  The residual row and column masses are then integral as well; matching a positive residual row to a positive residual column by their minimum mass, and iterating, gives an integral residual coupling supported on \(Q^{\mathsf c}\).  The reachable-set cut is a zero--one certificate.  Scaling back gives rational extremal couplings and the claimed integral representation.  This proves the complete-response portion of the open-ended question while leaving the overlapping-pattern frontier open.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: Suppose \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{feas}}<\infty\). On the feasible domain \(\Gamma\in[\Gamma_{\mathrm{feas}},\infty)\), the sets \(\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H)\) are nested and \(L_{\Gamma}\) is nonincreasing. If \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{maj}}<\infty\), the infimum in its definition is attained. Guaranteed strict majority benefit holds exactly for feasible \(\Gamma<\Gamma_{\mathrm{maj}}\), equivalently \(L_{\Gamma}>1/2\); at and above a finite \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{maj}}\), an observationally compatible law has \(\beta\le1/2\). If \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{maj}}=\infty\), every finite feasible sensitivity value guarantees \(\beta>1/2\). Values \(\Gamma<\Gamma_{\mathrm{feas}}\) are model-data incompatibilities and carry no majority-benefit interpretation. If the entries of \(H_a\) are rational, each finite threshold is computable to any prescribed positive rational tolerance by monotone rational linear-feasibility searches; when a threshold is infinite, the same search supplies valid increasing lower bounds but need not terminate with a certificate of infinity.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The unqualified computability sentence is not well posed for arbitrary real observed-law entries and cannot require a finite-tolerance approximation to the value infinity. Rational input permits exact LP feasibility at rational trial indices; finiteness permits bracketing and bisection. The mathematical threshold and majority characterization are unchanged.

proofs.proof_tex:
There is one positive-mass response stratum, whose mass is one; suppress its index.  Order the binary states as
\[
000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111.
\]
We use finite-table elimination for the arm completions and elementary transport-cut inequalities for the coupling.  All displayed masses in the definition of \(\mathsf W\) are conditional on one of the three active response patterns, each of which has probability \(1/3\).  At \(\Gamma=1\), the two sensitivity inequalities in \(\mathcal F_1(\mathsf W)\) coincide.  Hence, for each active pattern \(m\),
\[
\lambda_a(s,m)=\frac{1}{3}q_a(s),
\]
whereas a pattern having \(r_a(m)=0\) has \(\lambda_a(s,m)=0\).  Substitution in the projection equations shows that the corresponding pairwise marginals of \(q_a\) must equal the conditional projection tables displayed in the definition of \(\mathsf W\).  Conversely, any nonnegative \(q_a\) with those pairwise marginals, together with \(\lambda_a(s,m)=q_a(s)/3\) on the three active patterns and zero elsewhere, satisfies every arm-specific constraint.  Thus the following elimination is an exact characterization, rather than a relaxation.

Write \(p_s=6q_0(s)\) and put \(t=p_{000}\).  Successively using the control margins for coordinate pairs \(12\), \(13\), and \(23\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{001}&=1-t &&\text{from }p_{000}+p_{001}=1,\\
p_{010}&=1-t &&\text{from }p_{000}+p_{010}=1,\\
p_{100}&=2-t &&\text{from }p_{000}+p_{100}=2,\\
p_{011}&=t   &&\text{from }p_{010}+p_{011}=1,\\
p_{101}&=t   &&\text{from }p_{001}+p_{101}=1,\\
p_{110}&=1+t &&\text{from }p_{100}+p_{110}=3,\\
p_{111}&=1-t &&\text{from }p_{110}+p_{111}=2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The unused entries of all three pairwise tables are then satisfied by direct substitution.  Nonnegativity is equivalent to \(0\le t\le1\), and the entries sum to six.  Therefore every exact control completion, and no other one, is
\[
q_0^{,t}=\frac{1}{6}(t,1-t,1-t,t,2-t,t,1+t,1-t),
\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\]
For treatment, the zero cells in the \(12\) and \(13\) margins first force the four entries at \(000,001,010,011\) to vanish.  The \(23\) cells \(00\) and \(01\), the \(13\) cell \(10\), and the \(12\) cell \(11\) then give, respectively, the remaining masses \(1,1,2,2\) in units of \(1/6\).  Hence the treatment completion is unique:
\[
q_1=\frac{1}{6}(0,0,0,0,1,1,2,2).
\]
Both arm masses equal one.  Consequently a coupling exists for every \(t\in[0,1]\), for example the product coupling, and every such coupling has the support and normalization required by \(\mathcal F_1(\mathsf W)\).

We next bound the strict Pareto mass of an arbitrary coupling \(\pi\) of \(q_0^{,t}\) and \(q_1\).  Because \(111\) strictly dominates every binary state except itself,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi(R)
&\ge \sum_{s_0\ne111}\pi(s_0,111)\\
&=q_1(111)-\pi(111,111)\\
&\ge q_1(111)-q_0^{,t}(111)
=\frac{2}{6}-\frac{1-t}{6}
=\frac{1+t}{6}
\ge\frac16.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the lower transport-cut certificate.  At \(t=0\), define a coupling by the following nonzero entries, each of mass \(1/6\):
\[
001\mapsto110,
\quad010\mapsto101,
\quad100\mapsto100,
\quad100\mapsto111,
\quad110\mapsto110,
\quad111\mapsto111.
\]
Its row vector is \((0,1,1,0,2,0,1,1)/6=q_0^{,0}\), and its column vector is \((0,0,0,0,1,1,2,2)/6=q_1\).  Of its six mass units, only \(100\mapsto111\) belongs to \(R\).  With \(\lambda_a=q_a/3\) on the active patterns as above, this is a point of \(\mathcal F_1(\mathsf W)\), so the exact lower endpoint is \(1/6\).

For the upper endpoint, no pair beginning at \(111\) belongs to the strict relation \(R\).  Therefore
\[
\pi(R)\le1-q_0^{,t}(111)=\frac{5+t}{6}.
\]
There is a second cut.  Let \(A=\{011,101,110,111\}\).  A strict Pareto edge beginning in \(A\) can end only at \(111\), so the benefit mass originating in \(A\) is at most \(q_1(111)=2/6\).  The benefit mass originating outside \(A\) is at most the available row mass
\[
q_0^{,t}(A^{\mathsf c})
=\frac{t+(1-t)+(1-t)+(2-t)}6
=\frac{4-2t}{6}.
\]
It follows that
\[
\pi(R)\le\frac{6-2t}{6}=1-\frac{t}{3}.
\]
Combining the two cut certificates,
\[
\pi(R)\le
\min\!\left\{\frac{5+t}{6},\frac{6-2t}{6}\right\}
\le\frac89.
\]
Indeed, the first affine bound is at most \(8/9\) when \(t\le1/3\), and the second is at most \(8/9\) when \(t\ge1/3\).

At \(t=1/3\), the following are the nonzero entries of a coupling, now written with their masses:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
(s_0,s_1)&\pi(s_0,s_1)\\ \hline
(000,100)&1/18\\
(001,101)&1/9\\
(010,110)&1/9\\
(011,111)&1/18\\
(100,101)&1/18\\
(100,110)&2/9\\
(101,111)&1/18\\
(110,111)&2/9\\
(111,100)&1/9
\end{array}
\]
The row masses are
\[
\frac1{18}(1,2,2,1,5,1,4,2)=q_0^{,1/3},
\]
and the column masses are \((0,0,0,0,1,1,2,2)/6=q_1\).  Every displayed edge except \((111,100)\) lies in \(R\); hence its benefit mass is \(1-1/9=8/9\).  This proves that the upper certificate is attained.  Since \(\mathcal F_1(\mathsf W)\) is convex and the objective is linear, convex mixtures of the lower- and upper-attaining feasible points attain every intermediate value.  Thus the exact identified range is
\[
\mathcal I_1(\mathsf W)=[1/6,8/9].
\]

It remains to check the claimed strict enlargement under the rectangular relaxation.  The exact parameterization gives the coordinatewise control envelopes
\[
6\ell_0=(0,0,0,0,1,0,1,0),
\qquad
6u_0=(1,1,1,1,2,1,2,1),
\]
while treatment is point identified, so \(\ell_1=u_1=q_1\).  The proposed relaxed control vector
\[
\widetilde q_0=\frac16(1,1,1,0,2,0,1,0)
\]
lies coordinatewise between \(\ell_0\) and \(u_0\), is nonnegative, and sums to one.  Couple it to \(q_1\) using the six entries
\[
000\mapsto100,
\quad001\mapsto101,
\quad010\mapsto110,
\quad100\mapsto110,
\quad100\mapsto111,
\quad110\mapsto111,
\]
each with mass \(1/6\).  These entries have row marginal \(\widetilde q_0\) and column marginal \(q_1\), and every one is a strict Pareto edge.  This feasible point of \(\mathcal F^{\mathrm{rect}}_1(\mathsf W)\) has objective one; normalization makes one an upper bound for every coupling, so the relaxed upper endpoint equals one.

Finally, \(\widetilde q_0\) is not an exact control completion.  For response pattern \(110\), its projected mass at pair state \(00\) is
\[
\widetilde q_0(000)+\widetilde q_0(001)=\frac{2}{6},
\]
whereas the corresponding control table in \(\mathsf W\) requires \(1/6\).  Equivalently, with \(\lambda_0=\widetilde q_0/3\), the left side of the exact projection equation would be \(1/9\), while its observed-law right side is \((1/3)(1/6)=1/18\).  Thus the relaxed witness violates an overlapping pair-projection equality, proving that the increase from \(8/9\) to one is caused precisely by discarding the joint cross-state projection restrictions.
